# buf_redux - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/buf_redux/0.8.4/buf_redux/index.html

## Expand description

Drop-in replacements for buffered I/O types in `std::io`.

These replacements retain the method names/signatures and implemented traits of their stdlib counterparts, making replacement as simple as swapping the import of the type:

[§](https://docs.rs#bufreader)`BufReader`:

```
- use std::io::BufReader;
+ use buf_redux::BufReader;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#bufwriter)`BufWriter`:

```
- use std::io::BufWriter;
+ use buf_redux::BufWriter;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#linewriter)`LineWriter`:

```
- use std::io::LineWriter;
+ use buf_redux::LineWriter;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more-direct-control)More Direct Control

All replacement types provide methods to:

- Increase the capacity of the buffer
- Get the number of available bytes as well as the total capacity of the buffer
- Consume the wrapper without losing data

`BufReader` provides methods to:

- Access the buffer through an `&`-reference without performing I/O
- Force unconditional reads into the buffer
- Get a `Read`adapter which empties the buffer and then pulls from the inner reader directly
- Shuffle bytes down to the beginning of the buffer to make room for more reading
- Get inner reader and trimmed buffer with the remaining data

`BufWriter` and `LineWriter` provides methods to:

- Flush the buffer and unwrap the inner writer unconditionally.
- Get the inner writer and trimmed buffer with the unflushed data.

[§](https://docs.rs#more-sensible-and-customizable-buffering-behavior)More Sensible and Customizable Buffering Behavior

Tune the behavior of the buffer to your specific use-case using the types in the
[ policy module](https://docs.rs/policy/index.html):

-
Refine `BufReader`’s behavior by implementing the`ReaderPolicy`trait`MinBuffered`
-
Refine `BufWriter`’s behavior by implementing the [`WriterPolicy`trait] or use an existing implementation like`FlushOn``LineWriter`

[§](https://docs.rs#making-room)Making Room

The buffered types of this crate and their `std::io` counterparts, by default, use `Box<[u8]>`
as their buffer types ([ Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html) is included as well since it is used internally
by the other types in this crate).

When one of these types inserts bytes into its buffer, via `BufRead::fill_buf()` (implicitly
called by `Read::read()`) in `BufReader`’s case or `Write::write()` in `BufWriter`’s case,
the entire buffer is provided to be read/written into and the number of bytes written is saved.
The read/written data then resides in the `[0 .. bytes_inserted]` slice of the buffer.

When bytes are consumed from the buffer, via `BufRead::consume()` or `Write::flush()`,
the number of bytes consumed is added to the start of the slice such that the remaining
data resides in the `[bytes_consumed .. bytes_inserted]` slice of the buffer.

The `std::io` buffered types, and their counterparts in this crate with their default policies,
don’t have to deal with partially filled buffers as `BufReader` only reads when empty and
`BufWriter` only flushes when full.

However, because the replacements in this crate are capable of reading on-demand and flushing less than a full buffer, they can run out of room in their buffers to read/write data into even though there is technically free space, because this free space is at the head of the buffer where reading into it would cause the data in the buffer to become non-contiguous.

This isn’t technically a problem as the buffer could operate like `VecDeque` in `std` and return
both slices at once, but this would not fit all use-cases: the `Read::fill_buf()` interface only
allows one slice to be returned at a time so the older data would need to be completely consumed
before the newer data can be returned; `BufWriter` could support it as the `Write` interface
doesn’t make an opinion on how the buffer works, but because the data would be non-contiguous
it would require two flushes to get it all, which could degrade performance.

The obvious solution, then, is to move the existing data down to the beginning of the buffer
when there is no more room at the end so that more reads/writes into the buffer can be issued.
This works, and may suit some use-cases where the amount of data left is small and thus copying
it would be inexpensive, but it is non-optimal. However, this option is provided
as the `.make_room()` methods, and is utilized by [ policy::MinBuffered](https://docs.rs/policy/struct.MinBuffered.html)
and

[.](https://docs.rs/policy/struct.FlushExact.html)

`policy::FlushExact`[§](https://docs.rs#ringbuffers--slice-deque-feature)Ringbuffers / `slice-deque` Feature

Instead of moving data, however, it is also possible to use virtual-memory tricks to
allocate a ringbuffer that loops around on itself in memory and thus is always contiguous,
as described in [the Wikipedia article on Ringbuffers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_buffer#Optimization).

This is the exact trick used by [the  slice-deque crate](https://crates.io/crates/slice-deque),
which is now provided as an optional feature

`slice-deque` exposed via the
`new_ringbuf()` and `with_capacity_ringbuf()` constructors added to the buffered types here.
When a buffered type is constructed using one of these functions, `.make_room()` is turned into
a no-op as consuming bytes from the head of the buffer simultaneously makes room at the tail.
However, this has some caveats:-
It is only available on target platforms with virtual memory support, namely fully fledged OSes such as Windows and Unix-derivative platforms like Linux, OS X, BSD variants, etc.
-
The default capacity varies based on platform, and custom capacities are rounded up to a multiple of their minimum size, typically the page size of the platform. Windows’ minimum size is comparably quite large ( **64 KiB**) due to some legacy reasons, so this may be less optimal than the default capacity for a normal buffer (8 KiB) for some use-cases.
-
Due to the nature of the virtual-memory trick, the virtual address space the buffer allocates will be double its capacity. This means that your program will *appear*to use more memory than it would if it was using a normal buffer of the same capacity. The physical memory usage will be the same in both cases, but if address space is at a premium in your application (32-bit targets) then this may be a concern.

[178](https://docs.rs#178)/// A drop-in replacement for `std::io::BufReader` with more functionality.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)///
[180](https://docs.rs#180)/// Original method names/signatures and implemented traits are left untouched,
[181](https://docs.rs#181)/// making replacement as simple as swapping the import of the type.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)///
[183](https://docs.rs#183)/// By default this type implements the behavior of its `std` counterpart: it only reads into
[184](https://docs.rs#184)/// the buffer when it is empty.
[185](https://docs.rs#185)///
[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// To change this type's behavior, change the policy with [`.set_policy()`] using a type
[187](https://docs.rs#187)/// from the [`policy` module] or your own implementation of [`ReaderPolicy`].
[188](https://docs.rs#188)///
[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// Policies that perform alternating reads and consumes without completely emptying the buffer
[190](https://docs.rs#190)/// may benefit from using a ringbuffer via the [`new_ringbuf()`] and [`with_capacity_ringbuf()`]
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// constructors. Ringbuffers are only available on supported platforms with the
[192](https://docs.rs#192)/// `slice-deque` feature and have some other caveats; see [the crate root docs][ringbufs-root]
[193](https://docs.rs#193)/// for more details.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)///
[195](https://docs.rs#195)/// [`.set_policy()`]: BufReader::set_policy
[196](https://docs.rs#196)/// [`policy` module]: policy
[197](https://docs.rs#197)/// [`ReaderPolicy`]: policy::ReaderPolicy
[198](https://docs.rs#198)/// [`new_ringbuf()`]: BufReader::new_ringbuf
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// [`with_capacity_ringbuf()`]: BufReader::with_capacity_ringbuf
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// [ringbufs-root]: index.html#ringbuffers--slice-deque-feature
[201](https://docs.rs#201)pub struct BufReader<R, P = StdPolicy>{

[204](https://docs.rs#204)    inner: R,
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    policy: P,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)}

[213](https://docs.rs#213)    }
[214](https://docs.rs#214)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// Create a new `BufReader` wrapping `inner`, utilizing a buffer with a capacity
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// of *at least* `cap` bytes and the default [`ReaderPolicy`](policy::ReaderPolicy).

[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// allocator.

[221](https://docs.rs#221)        Self::with_buffer(Buffer::with_capacity(cap), inner)

[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// Create a new `BufReader` wrapping `inner`, utilizing a ringbuffer with the default capacity
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    /// and `ReaderPolicy`.
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    ///
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// A ringbuffer never has to move data to make room; consuming bytes from the head
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// simultaneously makes room at the tail. This is useful in conjunction with a policy like
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    /// [`MinBuffered`](policy::MinBuffered) to ensure there is always room to read more data
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// if necessary, without expensive copying operations.
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    ///
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// Only available on platforms with virtual memory support and with the `slice-deque` feature
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// enabled. The default capacity will differ between Windows and Unix-derivative targets.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// See [`Buffer::new_ringbuf()`](struct.Buffer.html#method.new_ringbuf)
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// or [the crate root docs](index.html#ringbuffers--slice-deque-feature) for more info.
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    #[cfg(feature = "slice-deque")]
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    pub fn new_ringbuf(inner: R) -> Self {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        Self::with_capacity_ringbuf(DEFAULT_BUF_SIZE, inner)
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    }
[240](https://docs.rs#240)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// Create a new `BufReader` wrapping `inner`, utilizing a ringbuffer with *at least* the given
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    /// capacity and the default `ReaderPolicy`.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    ///
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    /// A ringbuffer never has to move data to make room; consuming bytes from the head
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    /// simultaneously makes room at the tail. This is useful in conjunction with a policy like
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// [`MinBuffered`](policy::MinBuffered) to ensure there is always room to read more data
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// if necessary, without expensive copying operations.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    ///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    /// Only available on platforms with virtual memory support and with the `slice-deque` feature
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    /// enabled. The capacity will be rounded up to the minimum size for the target platform.
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    /// See [`Buffer::with_capacity_ringbuf()`](struct.Buffer.html#method.with_capacity_ringbuf)
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// or [the crate root docs](index.html#ringbuffers--slice-deque-feature) for more info.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    #[cfg(feature = "slice-deque")]
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    pub fn with_capacity_ringbuf(cap: usize, inner: R) -> Self {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)        Self::with_buffer(Buffer::with_capacity_ringbuf(cap), inner)
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    }
[257](https://docs.rs#257)
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    /// Wrap `inner` with an existing `Buffer` instance and the default `ReaderPolicy`.
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    ///
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// ### Note
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// Does **not** clear the buffer first! If there is data already in the buffer

[263](https://docs.rs#263)    pub fn with_buffer(buf: Buffer, inner: R) -> Self {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        BufReader {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            buf, inner, policy: StdPolicy

[362](https://docs.rs#362)impl<R: Read, P> BufReader<R, P> {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// Unconditionally perform a read into the buffer.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    ///
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// Does not invoke `ReaderPolicy` methods.
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    ///
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// If the read was successful, returns the number of bytes read.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    pub fn read_into_buf(&mut self) -> io::Result<usize> {
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        self.buf.read_from(&mut self.inner)
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    }
[371](https://docs.rs#371)
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// Box the inner reader without losing data.
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    pub fn boxed<'a>(self) -> BufReader<Box<Read + 'a>, P> where R: 'a {
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        let inner: Box<Read + 'a> = Box::new(self.inner);
[375](https://docs.rs#375)
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        BufReader {
[377](https://docs.rs#377)            inner,
[378](https://docs.rs#378)            buf: self.buf,
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            policy: self.policy,
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        }
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)}
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)impl<R: Read, P: ReaderPolicy> Read for BufReader<R, P> {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    fn read(&mut self, out: &mut [u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)        // If we don't have any buffered data and we're doing a read matching
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        // or exceeding the internal buffer's capacity, bypass the buffer.
[388](https://docs.rs#388)        if self.buf.is_empty() && out.len() >= self.buf.capacity() {
[389](https://docs.rs#389)            return self.inner.read(out);
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        }
[391](https://docs.rs#391)
[392](https://docs.rs#392)        let nread = self.fill_buf()?.read(out)?;
[393](https://docs.rs#393)        self.consume(nread);
[394](https://docs.rs#394)        Ok(nread)
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    }
[396](https://docs.rs#396)}
[397](https://docs.rs#397)
[398](https://docs.rs#398)impl<R: Read, P: ReaderPolicy> BufRead for BufReader<R, P> {
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    fn fill_buf(&mut self) -> io::Result<&[u8]> {
[400](https://docs.rs#400)        // If we've reached the end of our internal buffer then we need to fetch
[401](https://docs.rs#401)        // some more data from the underlying reader.
[402](https://docs.rs#402)        // This execution order is important; the policy may want to resize the buffer or move data
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        // before reading into it.
[404](https://docs.rs#404)        while self.should_read() && self.buf.usable_space() > 0 {
[405](https://docs.rs#405)            if self.read_into_buf()? == 0 { break; };
[406](https://docs.rs#406)        }
[407](https://docs.rs#407)
[408](https://docs.rs#408)        Ok(self.buffer())
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    }
[410](https://docs.rs#410)
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    fn consume(&mut self, mut amt: usize) {
[412](https://docs.rs#412)        amt = cmp::min(amt, self.buf_len());
[413](https://docs.rs#413)        self.buf.consume(amt);
[414](https://docs.rs#414)        self.policy.after_consume(&mut self.buf, amt);
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    }
[416](https://docs.rs#416)}
[417](https://docs.rs#417)
[418](https://docs.rs#418)impl<R: fmt::Debug, P: fmt::Debug> fmt::Debug for BufReader<R, P> {
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    fn fmt(&self, fmt: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[420](https://docs.rs#420)        fmt.debug_struct("buf_redux::BufReader")
[421](https://docs.rs#421)            .field("reader", &self.inner)
[422](https://docs.rs#422)            .field("buf_len", &self.buf_len())
[423](https://docs.rs#423)            .field("capacity", &self.capacity())
[424](https://docs.rs#424)            .field("policy", &self.policy)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)            .finish()
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    }
[427](https://docs.rs#427)}
[428](https://docs.rs#428)
[429](https://docs.rs#429)impl<R: Seek, P: ReaderPolicy> Seek for BufReader<R, P> {
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// Seek to an ofPet, in bytes, in the underlying reader.
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    ///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// The position used for seeking with `SeekFrom::Current(_)` is the
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// position the underlying reader would be at if the `BufReader` had no
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// internal buffer.
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    ///
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// Seeking always discards the internal buffer, even if the seek position
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// would otherwise fall within it. This guarantees that calling
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// `.unwrap()` immediately after a seek yields the underlying reader at
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// the same position.
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    ///
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// See `std::io::Seek` for more details.
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    ///
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    /// Note: In the edge case where you're seeking with `SeekFrom::Current(n)`
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// where `n` minus the internal buffer length underflows an `i64`, two
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    /// seeks will be performed instead of one. If the second seek returns
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// `Err`, the underlying reader will be left at the same position it would
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// have if you seeked to `SeekFrom::Current(0)`.
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    fn seek(&mut self, pos: SeekFrom) -> io::Result<u64> {
[449](https://docs.rs#449)        let result: u64;
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        if let SeekFrom::Current(n) = pos {
[451](https://docs.rs#451)            let remainder = self.buf_len() as i64;
[452](https://docs.rs#452)            // it should be safe to assume that remainder fits within an i64 as the alternative
[453](https://docs.rs#453)            // means we managed to allocate 8 ebibytes and that's absurd.
[454](https://docs.rs#454)            // But it's not out of the realm of possibility for some weird underlying reader to
[455](https://docs.rs#455)            // support seeking by i64::min_value() so we need to handle underflow when subtracting
[456](https://docs.rs#456)            // remainder.
[457](https://docs.rs#457)            if let Some(offset) = n.checked_sub(remainder) {
[458](https://docs.rs#458)                result = self.inner.seek(SeekFrom::Current(offset))?;
[459](https://docs.rs#459)            } else {
[460](https://docs.rs#460)                // seek backwards by our remainder, and then by the offset
[461](https://docs.rs#461)                self.inner.seek(SeekFrom::Current(-remainder))?;
[462](https://docs.rs#462)                self.buf.clear(); // empty the buffer
[463](https://docs.rs#463)                result = self.inner.seek(SeekFrom::Current(n))?;
[464](https://docs.rs#464)            }
[465](https://docs.rs#465)        } else {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)            // Seeking with Start/End doesn't care about our buffer length.
[467](https://docs.rs#467)            result = self.inner.seek(pos)?;
[468](https://docs.rs#468)        }
[469](https://docs.rs#469)        self.buf.clear();
[470](https://docs.rs#470)        Ok(result)
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    }
[472](https://docs.rs#472)}
[473](https://docs.rs#473)
[474](https://docs.rs#474)/// A drop-in replacement for `std::io::BufWriter` with more functionality.
[475](https://docs.rs#475)///
[476](https://docs.rs#476)/// Original method names/signatures and implemented traits are left untouched,
[477](https://docs.rs#477)/// making replacement as simple as swapping the import of the type.
[478](https://docs.rs#478)///
[479](https://docs.rs#479)/// By default this type implements the behavior of its `std` counterpart: it only flushes
[480](https://docs.rs#480)/// the buffer if an incoming write is larger than the remaining space.
[481](https://docs.rs#481)///
[482](https://docs.rs#482)/// To change this type's behavior, change the policy with [`.set_policy()`] using a type
[483](https://docs.rs#483)/// from the [`policy` module] or your own implentation of [`WriterPolicy`].
[484](https://docs.rs#484)///
[485](https://docs.rs#485)/// Policies that perform alternating writes and flushes without completely emptying the buffer
[486](https://docs.rs#486)/// may benefit from using a ringbuffer via the [`new_ringbuf()`] and [`with_capacity_ringbuf()`]
[487](https://docs.rs#487)/// constructors. Ringbuffers are only available on supported platforms with the
[488](https://docs.rs#488)/// `slice-deque` feature and have some caveats; see [the docs at the crate root][ringbufs-root]
[489](https://docs.rs#489)/// for more details.
[490](https://docs.rs#490)///
[491](https://docs.rs#491)/// [`.set_policy()`]: BufWriter::set_policy

[520](https://docs.rs#520)    /// Create a new `BufWriter` wrapping `inner`, utilizing a ringbuffer with the default
[521](https://docs.rs#521)    /// capacity and [`WriterPolicy`](policy::WriterPolicy).
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    ///
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    /// A ringbuffer never has to move data to make room; consuming bytes from the head
[524](https://docs.rs#524)    /// simultaneously makes room at the tail. This is useful in conjunction with a policy like
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    ///  [`FlushExact`](policy::FlushExact) to ensure there is always room to write more data if
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    /// necessary, without expensive copying operations.
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    ///
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    /// Only available on platforms with virtual memory support and with the `slice-deque` feature
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    /// enabled. The default capacity will differ between Windows and Unix-derivative targets.
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    /// See [`Buffer::new_ringbuf()`](Buffer::new_ringbuf)
[531](https://docs.rs#531)    /// or [the crate root docs](index.html#ringbuffers--slice-deque-feature) for more info.
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    #[cfg(feature = "slice-deque")]
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    pub fn new_ringbuf(inner: W) -> Self {
[534](https://docs.rs#534)        Self::with_buffer(Buffer::new_ringbuf(), inner)
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    }
[536](https://docs.rs#536)
[537](https://docs.rs#537)    /// Create a new `BufWriter` wrapping `inner`, utilizing a ringbuffer with *at least* `cap`
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    /// capacity and the default [`WriterPolicy`](policy::WriterPolicy).
[539](https://docs.rs#539)    ///
[540](https://docs.rs#540)    /// A ringbuffer never has to move data to make room; consuming bytes from the head
[541](https://docs.rs#541)    /// simultaneously makes room at the tail. This is useful in conjunction with a policy like
[542](https://docs.rs#542)    /// [`FlushExact`](policy::FlushExact) to ensure there is always room to write more data if
[543](https://docs.rs#543)    /// necessary, without expensive copying operations.

[545](https://docs.rs#545)    /// Only available on platforms with virtual memory support and with the `slice-deque` feature

[570](https://docs.rs#570)        let panicked = self.panicked;
[571](https://docs.rs#571)        let (inner, buf) = self.into_inner_();

[626](https://docs.rs#626)    /// Consume `self` and return both the underlying writer and the buffer
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    pub fn into_inner_with_buffer(self) -> (W, Buffer) {
[628](https://docs.rs#628)        self.into_inner_()
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    }
[630](https://docs.rs#630)
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    // copy the fields out and forget `self` to avoid dropping twice
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    fn into_inner_(self) -> (W, Buffer) {
[633](https://docs.rs#633)        let s = ManuallyDrop::new(self);
[634](https://docs.rs#634)        unsafe {
[635](https://docs.rs#635)            // safe because we immediately forget `self`
[636](https://docs.rs#636)            let inner = ptr::read(&s.inner);
[637](https://docs.rs#637)            let buf = ptr::read(&s.buf);
[638](https://docs.rs#638)            (inner, buf)
[639](https://docs.rs#639)        }
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    }
[641](https://docs.rs#641)
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    fn flush_buf(&mut self, amt: usize) -> io::Result<()> {
[643](https://docs.rs#643)        if amt == 0 || amt > self.buf.len() { return Ok(()) }
[644](https://docs.rs#644)
[645](https://docs.rs#645)        self.panicked = true;
[646](https://docs.rs#646)        let ret = self.buf.write_max(amt, &mut self.inner);
[647](https://docs.rs#647)        self.panicked = false;
[648](https://docs.rs#648)        ret
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    }

[652](https://docs.rs#652)impl<W: Write, P: WriterPolicy> BufWriter<W, P> {
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    /// Flush the buffer and unwrap, returning the inner writer on success,
[654](https://docs.rs#654)    /// or a type wrapping `self` plus the error otherwise.
[655](https://docs.rs#655)    pub fn into_inner(mut self) -> Result<W, IntoInnerError<Self>> {
[656](https://docs.rs#656)        match self.flush() {
[657](https://docs.rs#657)            Err(e) => Err(IntoInnerError(self, e)),
[658](https://docs.rs#658)            Ok(()) => Ok(self.into_inner_().0),
[659](https://docs.rs#659)        }
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    }
[661](https://docs.rs#661)
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    /// Flush the buffer and unwrap, returning the inner writer and
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    /// any error encountered during flushing.
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    pub fn into_inner_with_err(mut self) -> (W, Option<io::Error>) {
[665](https://docs.rs#665)        let err = self.flush().err();
[666](https://docs.rs#666)        (self.into_inner_().0, err)
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    }
[668](https://docs.rs#668)}
[669](https://docs.rs#669)
[670](https://docs.rs#670)impl<W: Write, P: WriterPolicy> Write for BufWriter<W, P> {
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    fn write(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> io::Result<usize> {
[672](https://docs.rs#672)        let flush_amt = self.policy.before_write(&mut self.buf, buf.len()).0;
[673](https://docs.rs#673)        self.flush_buf(flush_amt)?;
[674](https://docs.rs#674)
[675](https://docs.rs#675)        let written = if self.buf.is_empty() && buf.len() >= self.buf.capacity() {
[676](https://docs.rs#676)            self.panicked = true;
[677](https://docs.rs#677)            let result = self.inner.write(buf);
[678](https://docs.rs#678)            self.panicked = false;
[679](https://docs.rs#679)            result?
[680](https://docs.rs#680)        } else {
[681](https://docs.rs#681)            self.buf.copy_from_slice(buf)
[682](https://docs.rs#682)        };
[683](https://docs.rs#683)
[684](https://docs.rs#684)        let flush_amt = self.policy.after_write(&self.buf).0;
[685](https://docs.rs#685)
[686](https://docs.rs#686)        let _ = self.flush_buf(flush_amt);
[687](https://docs.rs#687)
[688](https://docs.rs#688)        Ok(written)
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    }
[690](https://docs.rs#690)
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    fn flush(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
[692](https://docs.rs#692)        let flush_amt = self.buf.len();
[693](https://docs.rs#693)        self.flush_buf(flush_amt)?;
[694](https://docs.rs#694)        self.inner.flush()
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    }
[696](https://docs.rs#696)}

[698](https://docs.rs#698)impl<W: Write + Seek, P: WriterPolicy> Seek for BufWriter<W, P> {
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    /// Seek to the ofPet, in bytes, in the underlying writer.
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    ///
[701](https://docs.rs#701)    /// Seeking always writes out the internal buffer before seeking.
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    fn seek(&mut self, pos: SeekFrom) -> io::Result<u64> {
[703](https://docs.rs#703)        self.flush().and_then(|_| self.get_mut().seek(pos))
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    }

[717](https://docs.rs#717)
[718](https://docs.rs#718)/// Attempt to flush the buffer to the underlying writer.
[719](https://docs.rs#719)///
[720](https://docs.rs#720)/// If an error occurs, the thread-local handler is invoked, if one was previously
[721](https://docs.rs#721)/// set by [`set_drop_err_handler`](set_drop_err_handler) for this thread.
[722](https://docs.rs#722)impl<W: Write, P> Drop for BufWriter<W, P> {
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    fn drop(&mut self) {
[724](https://docs.rs#724)        if !self.panicked {
[725](https://docs.rs#725)            // instead of ignoring a failed flush, call the handler
[726](https://docs.rs#726)            let buf_len = self.buf.len();
[727](https://docs.rs#727)            if let Err(err) = self.flush_buf(buf_len) {
[728](https://docs.rs#728)                DROP_ERR_HANDLER.with(|deh| {
[729](https://docs.rs#729)                    (*deh.borrow())(&mut self.inner, &mut self.buf, err)
[730](https://docs.rs#730)                });
[731](https://docs.rs#731)            }
[732](https://docs.rs#732)        }
[733](https://docs.rs#733)    }

[925](https://docs.rs#925)    /// Allocate a buffer with *at least* the given capacity that never needs to move data to

[998](https://docs.rs#998)    /// Ensure space for at least `additional` more bytes in the buffer.
[999](https://docs.rs#999)    ///
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)    /// This is a no-op if `usable_space() >= additional`. Note that this will reallocate
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)    /// even if there is enough free space at the head of the buffer for `additional` bytes,
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)    /// because that free space is not at the tail where it can be read into.
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)    /// If you prefer copying data down in the buffer before attempting to reallocate you may wish
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)    /// to call `.make_room()` first.
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)    ///
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)    /// ### Panics
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)    /// If `self.capacity() + additional` overflows.
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)    pub fn reserve(&mut self, additional: usize) {
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)        // Returns `true` if we reallocated out-of-place and thus need to re-zero.
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)        if self.buf.reserve(additional) {
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)            self.zeroed = 0;
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)        }
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)    }

[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)    /// Read from `rdr`, returning the number of bytes read or any errors.
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)    ///
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)    /// If there is no more room at the head of the buffer, this will return `Ok(0)`.
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)    ///
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)    /// Uses `Read::initializer()` to initialize the buffer if the `nightly`
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)    /// feature is enabled, otherwise the buffer is zeroed if it has never been written.
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)    ///
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)    /// ### Panics
[1033](https://docs.rs#1033)    /// If the returned count from `rdr.read()` overflows the tail cursor of this buffer.
[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)    pub fn read_from<R: Read + ?Sized>(&mut self, rdr: &mut R) -> io::Result<usize> {
[1035](https://docs.rs#1035)        if self.usable_space() == 0 {
[1036](https://docs.rs#1036)            return Ok(0);
[1037](https://docs.rs#1037)        }
[1038](https://docs.rs#1038)
[1039](https://docs.rs#1039)        let cap = self.capacity();
[1040](https://docs.rs#1040)        if self.zeroed < cap {
[1041](https://docs.rs#1041)            unsafe {
[1042](https://docs.rs#1042)                let buf = self.buf.write_buf();
[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)                init_buffer(&rdr, buf);
[1044](https://docs.rs#1044)            }
[1045](https://docs.rs#1045)
[1046](https://docs.rs#1046)            self.zeroed = cap;
[1047](https://docs.rs#1047)        }
[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)        let read = {
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)            let mut buf = unsafe { self.buf.write_buf() };
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051)            rdr.read(buf)?
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)        };
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)        unsafe {
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)            self.buf.bytes_written(read);
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)        }
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)        Ok(read)
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)    }
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)    /// Copy from `src` to the tail of this buffer. Returns the number of bytes copied.
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)    ///
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)    /// This will **not** grow the buffer if `src` is larger than `self.usable_space()`; instead,
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)    /// it will fill the usable space and return the number of bytes copied. If there is no usable
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)    /// space, this returns 0.
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)    pub fn copy_from_slice(&mut self, src: &[u8]) -> usize {
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)        let len = unsafe {
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)            let mut buf = self.buf.write_buf();
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)            let len = cmp::min(buf.len(), src.len());
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)            buf[..len].copy_from_slice(&src[..len]);
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)            len
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)        };
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)        unsafe {
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)            self.buf.bytes_written(len);
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)        }
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)        len
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)    }
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)    /// Write bytes from this buffer to `wrt`. Returns the number of bytes written or any errors.
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)    ///
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)    /// If the buffer is empty, returns `Ok(0)`.
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)    ///
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)    /// ### Panics
[1086](https://docs.rs#1086)    /// If the count returned by `wrt.write()` would cause the head cursor to overflow or pass
[1087](https://docs.rs#1087)    /// the tail cursor if added to it.
[1088](https://docs.rs#1088)    pub fn write_to<W: Write + ?Sized>(&mut self, wrt: &mut W) -> io::Result<usize> {
[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)        if self.len() == 0 {
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)            return Ok(0);
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)        }
[1092](https://docs.rs#1092)
[1093](https://docs.rs#1093)        let written = wrt.write(self.buf())?;
[1094](https://docs.rs#1094)        self.consume(written);
[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)        Ok(written)
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)    }
[1097](https://docs.rs#1097)
[1098](https://docs.rs#1098)    /// Write, at most, the given number of bytes from this buffer to `wrt`, continuing
[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)    /// to write and ignoring interrupts until the number is reached or the buffer is empty.
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)    ///
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)    /// ### Panics
[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)    /// If the count returned by `wrt.write()` would cause the head cursor to overflow or pass
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)    /// the tail cursor if added to it.
[1104](https://docs.rs#1104)    pub fn write_max<W: Write + ?Sized>(&mut self, mut max: usize, wrt: &mut W) -> io::Result<()> {
[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)        while self.len() > 0 && max > 0 {
[1106](https://docs.rs#1106)            let len = cmp::min(self.len(), max);
[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)            let n = match wrt.write(&self.buf()[..len]) {
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)                Ok(0) => return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::WriteZero,
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)                                                   "Buffer::write_all() got zero-sized write")),
[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)                Ok(n) => n,
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)                Err(ref e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::Interrupted => continue,
[1112](https://docs.rs#1112)                Err(e) => return Err(e),
[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)            };
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)            self.consume(n);
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)            max = max.saturating_sub(n);
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)        }
[1118](https://docs.rs#1118)
[1119](https://docs.rs#1119)        Ok(())
[1120](https://docs.rs#1120)    }
[1121](https://docs.rs#1121)
[1122](https://docs.rs#1122)    /// Write all bytes in this buffer to `wrt`, ignoring interrupts. Continues writing until
[1123](https://docs.rs#1123)    /// the buffer is empty or an error is returned.
[1124](https://docs.rs#1124)    ///
[1125](https://docs.rs#1125)    /// ### Panics
[1126](https://docs.rs#1126)    /// If `self.write_to(wrt)` panics.
[1127](https://docs.rs#1127)    pub fn write_all<W: Write + ?Sized>(&mut self, wrt: &mut W) -> io::Result<()> {
[1128](https://docs.rs#1128)        while self.len() > 0 {
[1129](https://docs.rs#1129)            match self.write_to(wrt) {
[1130](https://docs.rs#1130)                Ok(0) => return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::WriteZero,
[1131](https://docs.rs#1131)                                                   "Buffer::write_all() got zero-sized write")),
[1132](https://docs.rs#1132)                Ok(_) => (),
[1133](https://docs.rs#1133)                Err(ref e) if e.kind() == io::ErrorKind::Interrupted => (),
[1134](https://docs.rs#1134)                Err(e) => return Err(e),
[1135](https://docs.rs#1135)            }
[1136](https://docs.rs#1136)        }
[1137](https://docs.rs#1137)
[1138](https://docs.rs#1138)        Ok(())
[1139](https://docs.rs#1139)    }
[1140](https://docs.rs#1140)
[1141](https://docs.rs#1141)    /// Copy bytes to `out` from this buffer, returning the number of bytes written.
[1142](https://docs.rs#1142)    pub fn copy_to_slice(&mut self, out: &mut [u8]) -> usize {
[1143](https://docs.rs#1143)        let len = {
[1144](https://docs.rs#1144)            let buf = self.buf();
[1145](https://docs.rs#1145)
[1146](https://docs.rs#1146)            let len = cmp::min(buf.len(), out.len());
[1147](https://docs.rs#1147)            out[..len].copy_from_slice(&buf[..len]);
[1148](https://docs.rs#1148)            len
[1149](https://docs.rs#1149)        };
[1150](https://docs.rs#1150)
[1151](https://docs.rs#1151)        self.consume(len);
[1152](https://docs.rs#1152)
[1153](https://docs.rs#1153)        len
[1154](https://docs.rs#1154)    }
[1155](https://docs.rs#1155)
[1156](https://docs.rs#1156)    /// Push `bytes` to the end of the buffer, growing it if necessary.
[1157](https://docs.rs#1157)    ///
[1158](https://docs.rs#1158)    /// If you prefer moving bytes down in the buffer to reallocating, you may wish to call
[1159](https://docs.rs#1159)    /// `.make_room()` first.
[1160](https://docs.rs#1160)    pub fn push_bytes(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) {
[1161](https://docs.rs#1161)        let s_len = bytes.len();
[1162](https://docs.rs#1162)
[1163](https://docs.rs#1163)        if self.usable_space() < s_len {
[1164](https://docs.rs#1164)            self.reserve(s_len * 2);
[1165](https://docs.rs#1165)        }
[1166](https://docs.rs#1166)
[1167](https://docs.rs#1167)        unsafe {
[1168](https://docs.rs#1168)            self.buf.write_buf()[..s_len].copy_from_slice(bytes);
[1169](https://docs.rs#1169)            self.buf.bytes_written(s_len);
[1170](https://docs.rs#1170)        }
[1171](https://docs.rs#1171)    }
[1172](https://docs.rs#1172)
[1173](https://docs.rs#1173)    /// Consume `amt` bytes from the head of this buffer.
[1174](https://docs.rs#1174)    pub fn consume(&mut self, amt: usize) {
[1175](https://docs.rs#1175)        self.buf.consume(amt);
[1176](https://docs.rs#1176)    }
[1177](https://docs.rs#1177)
[1178](https://docs.rs#1178)    /// Empty this buffer by consuming all bytes.
[1179](https://docs.rs#1179)    pub fn clear(&mut self) {
[1180](https://docs.rs#1180)        let buf_len = self.len();
[1181](https://docs.rs#1181)        self.consume(buf_len);
[1182](https://docs.rs#1182)    }

[1185](https://docs.rs#1185)impl fmt::Debug for Buffer {

# buf_redux::policy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/buf_redux/0.8.4/buf_redux/policy/index.html

## Expand description

Types which can be used to tune the behavior of `BufReader` and `BufWriter`.

Some simple policies are provided for your convenience. You may prefer to create your own types and implement the traits for them instead.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DoRead](https://docs.rs/struct.DoRead.html)
- Flag for `ReaderPolicy`methods to signal whether or not`BufReader`should read into the buffer.
- [Flush](https://docs.rs/struct.FlushAmt.html)- Amt
- Flag for `WriterPolicy`methods to tell`BufWriter`how many bytes to flush to the underlying reader.
- [Flush](https://docs.rs/struct.FlushAtLeast.html)- AtLeast
- Flush the buffer if it contains at least the given number of bytes.
- [Flush](https://docs.rs/struct.FlushExact.html)- Exact
- Only ever flush exactly the given number of bytes, until the writer is empty.
- [FlushOn](https://docs.rs/struct.FlushOn.html)
- Flush the buffer if it contains the given byte.
- [Flush](https://docs.rs/struct.FlushOnNewline.html)- OnNewline
- Flush the buffer if it contains a newline (`\n`).
- [MinBuffered](https://docs.rs/struct.MinBuffered.html)
- A policy for `BufReader`
- [StdPolicy](https://docs.rs/struct.StdPolicy.html)
- Default policy for both `BufReader`and`BufWriter`that reproduces the behaviors of their`std::io`counterparts:

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Reader](https://docs.rs/trait.ReaderPolicy.html)- Policy
- Trait that governs `BufReader`’s behavior.
- [Writer](https://docs.rs/trait.WriterPolicy.html)- Policy
- A trait which tells `BufWriter`when to flush.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/policy.rs.html#58)#### fn [before_read](https://docs.rs#method.before_read)(&mut self, buffer: &mut [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)) -> [DoRead](https://docs.rs/struct.DoRead.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/policy.rs.html#58)

#### fn [before_read](https://docs.rs#method.before_read)(&mut self, buffer: &mut [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)) -> [DoRead](https://docs.rs/struct.DoRead.html)

Consulted before attempting to read into the buffer.

Return `DoRead(true)` to issue a read into the buffer before reading data out of it,
or `DoRead(false)` to read from the buffer as it is, even if it’s empty.
`do_read!()` is provided as a shorthand.

If there is no room in the buffer after this method is called,
the buffer will not be read into (so if the buffer is full but you want more data
you should call `.make_room()` or reserve more space). If there *is* room, `BufReader` will
attempt to read into the buffer. If successful (`Ok(x)` where `x > 0` is returned), this
method will be consulted again for another read attempt.

By default, this implements `std::io::BufReader`’s behavior: only read into the buffer if
it is empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

If the read will ignore the buffer entirely (if the buffer is empty and the amount to be
read matches or exceeds its capacity) or if `BufReader::read_into_buf()` was called to force
a read into the buffer manually, this method will not be called.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/policy.rs.html#66)#### fn [after_consume](https://docs.rs#method.after_consume)(&mut self, _buffer: &mut [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html), _amt: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/policy.rs.html#66)

#### fn [after_consume](https://docs.rs#method.after_consume)(&mut self, _buffer: &mut [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html), _amt: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

Called after bytes are consumed from the buffer.

Supplies the true amount consumed if the amount passed to `BufReader::consume`
was in excess.

This is a no-op by default.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# MinBuffered in buf_redux::policy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/buf_redux/0.8.4/buf_redux/policy/struct.MinBuffered.html

`pub struct MinBuffered(pub `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html));## Expand description

A policy for [ BufReader](https://docs.rs/struct.BufReader.html) which ensures there is at least the given number of
bytes in  the buffer, failing this only if the reader is at EOF.

If the minimum buffer length is greater than the buffer capacity, it will be resized.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use buf_redux::BufReader;
use buf_redux::policy::MinBuffered;
use std::io::{BufRead, Cursor};

let data = (1 .. 16).collect::<Vec<u8>>();
// normally you should use `BufReader::new()` or give a capacity of several KiB or more
let mut reader = BufReader::with_capacity(8, Cursor::new(data))
    // always at least 4 bytes in the buffer (or until the source is empty)
    .set_policy(MinBuffered(4)); // always at least 4 bytes in the buffer
// first buffer fill, same as `std::io::BufReader`
assert_eq!(reader.fill_buf().unwrap(), &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]);
reader.consume(3);
// enough data in the buffer, another read isn't done yet
assert_eq!(reader.fill_buf().unwrap(), &[4, 5, 6, 7, 8]);
reader.consume(4);
// `std::io::BufReader` would return `&[8]`
assert_eq!(reader.fill_buf().unwrap(), &[8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]);
reader.consume(5);
// no data left in the reader
assert_eq!(reader.fill_buf().unwrap(), &[13, 14, 15]);
```

# Buffer in buf_redux - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/buf_redux/0.8.4/buf_redux/struct.Buffer.html

`pub struct Buffer { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A deque-like datastructure for managing bytes.

Supports interacting via I/O traits like `Read` and `Write`, and direct access.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/lib.rs.html#899-904)#### pub fn [with_capacity](https://docs.rs#method.with_capacity)(cap: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/lib.rs.html#899-904)

#### pub fn [with_capacity](https://docs.rs#method.with_capacity)(cap: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> Self

Create a new buffer with *at least* the given capacity.

If the global allocator returns extra capacity, `Buffer` will use all of it.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/lib.rs.html#921-923)#### pub fn [new_ringbuf](https://docs.rs#method.new_ringbuf)() -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/lib.rs.html#921-923)

#### pub fn [new_ringbuf](https://docs.rs#method.new_ringbuf)() -> Self

Allocate a buffer with a default capacity that never needs to move data to make room (consuming from the head simultaneously makes more room at the tail).

The default capacity varies based on the target platform:

- Unix-derivative platforms; Linux, OS X, BSDs, etc: **8KiB**(the default buffer size for`std::io`buffered types)
- Windows: **64KiB**because of legacy reasons, of course (see below)

Only available on platforms with virtual memory support and with the `slice-deque` feature
enabled. The current platforms that are supported/tested are listed
[in the README for the  slice-deque crate](https://github.com/gnzlbg/slice_deque#platform-support).

#### pub fn [with_capacity_ringbuf](https://docs.rs#method.with_capacity_ringbuf)(cap: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> Self

Allocate a buffer with *at least* the given capacity that never needs to move data to
make room (consuming from the head simultaneously makes more room at the tail).

The capacity will be rounded up to the minimum size for the current target:

- Unix-derivative platforms; Linux, OS X, BSDs, etc: the next multiple of the page size (typically 4KiB but can vary based on system configuration)
- Windows: the next muliple of **64KiB**; see[this Microsoft dev blog post](https://blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20031008-00/?p=42223)for why it’s 64KiB and not the page size (TL;DR: Alpha AXP needs it and it’s applied on all targets for consistency/portability)

Only available on platforms with virtual memory support and with the `slice-deque` feature
enabled. The current platforms that are supported/tested are listed
[in the README for the  slice-deque crate](https://github.com/gnzlbg/slice_deque#platform-support).

Return the number of bytes currently in this buffer.

Equivalent to `self.buf().len()`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/lib.rs.html#968-970)#### pub fn [usable_space](https://docs.rs#method.usable_space)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

#### pub fn [usable_space](https://docs.rs#method.usable_space)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Return the number of bytes that can be read into this buffer before it needs to grow or the data in the buffer needs to be moved.

This may not constitute all free space in the buffer if bytes have been consumed
from the head. Use `free_space()` to determine the total free space in the buffer.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/lib.rs.html#977-979)#### pub fn [free_space](https://docs.rs#method.free_space)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/buf_redux/lib.rs.html#977-979)

#### pub fn [free_space](https://docs.rs#method.free_space)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Returns the total amount of free space in the buffer, including bytes already consumed from the head.

This will be greater than or equal to `usable_space()`. On supported platforms
with the `slice-deque` feature enabled, it should be equal.

Returns `true` if there are no bytes in the buffer, false otherwise.

Move bytes down in the buffer to maximize usable space.

This is a no-op on supported platforms with the `slice-deque` feature enabled.

Ensure space for at least `additional` more bytes in the buffer.

This is a no-op if `usable_space() >= additional`. Note that this will reallocate
even if there is enough free space at the head of the buffer for `additional` bytes,
because that free space is not at the tail where it can be read into.
If you prefer copying data down in the buffer before attempting to reallocate you may wish
to call `.make_room()` first.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If `self.capacity() + additional` overflows.

Get an immutable slice of the available bytes in this buffer.

Call `.consume()` to remove bytes from the beginning of this slice.

Get a mutable slice representing the available bytes in this buffer.

Call `.consume()` to remove bytes from the beginning of this slice.

Read from `rdr`, returning the number of bytes read or any errors.

If there is no more room at the head of the buffer, this will return `Ok(0)`.

Uses `Read::initializer()` to initialize the buffer if the `nightly`
feature is enabled, otherwise the buffer is zeroed if it has never been written.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

If the returned count from `rdr.read()` overflows the tail cursor of this buffer.

A drop-in replacement for `std::io::BufReader` with more functionality.

Original method names/signatures and implemented traits are left untouched, making replacement as simple as swapping the import of the type.

By default this type implements the behavior of its `std` counterpart: it only reads into
the buffer when it is empty.

To change this type’s behavior, change the policy with [ .set_policy()](https://docs.rs/struct.BufReader.html#method.set_policy) using a type
from the

[or your own implementation of](https://docs.rs/policy/index.html)

`policy` module[.](https://docs.rs/policy/trait.ReaderPolicy.html)

`ReaderPolicy`Policies that perform alternating reads and consumes without completely emptying the buffer
may benefit from using a ringbuffer via the [ new_ringbuf()](https://docs.rs/struct.BufReader.html#method.new_ringbuf) and

[constructors. Ringbuffers are only available on supported platforms with the](https://docs.rs/struct.BufReader.html#method.with_capacity_ringbuf)

`with_capacity_ringbuf()``slice-deque` feature and have some other caveats; see [the crate root docs](https://docs.rs/index.html#ringbuffers--slice-deque-feature)for more details.

#### pub fn [new_ringbuf](https://docs.rs#method.new_ringbuf)(inner: R) -> Self

Create a new `BufReader` wrapping `inner`, utilizing a ringbuffer with the default capacity
and `ReaderPolicy`.

A ringbuffer never has to move data to make room; consuming bytes from the head
simultaneously makes room at the tail. This is useful in conjunction with a policy like
[ MinBuffered](https://docs.rs/policy/struct.MinBuffered.html) to ensure there is always room to read more data
if necessary, without expensive copying operations.

Only available on platforms with virtual memory support and with the `slice-deque` feature
enabled. The default capacity will differ between Windows and Unix-derivative targets.

The position used for seeking with `SeekFrom::Current(_)` is the
position the underlying reader would be at if the `BufReader` had no
internal buffer.

Seeking always discards the internal buffer, even if the seek position
would otherwise fall within it. This guarantees that calling
`.unwrap()` immediately after a seek yields the underlying reader at
the same position.

See `std::io::Seek` for more details.

Note: In the edge case where you’re seeking with `SeekFrom::Current(n)`
where `n` minus the internal buffer length underflows an `i64`, two
seeks will be performed instead of one. If the second seek returns
`Err`, the underlying reader will be left at the same position it would
have if you seeked to `SeekFrom::Current(0)`.

# buf_redux - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/buf_redux/latest/buf_redux/

## Expand description

Drop-in replacements for buffered I/O types in `std::io`.

These replacements retain the method names/signatures and implemented traits of their stdlib counterparts, making replacement as simple as swapping the import of the type:

[§](https://docs.rs#bufreader)`BufReader`:

```
- use std::io::BufReader;
+ use buf_redux::BufReader;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#bufwriter)`BufWriter`:

```
- use std::io::BufWriter;
+ use buf_redux::BufWriter;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#linewriter)`LineWriter`:

```
- use std::io::LineWriter;
+ use buf_redux::LineWriter;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more-direct-control)More Direct Control

All replacement types provide methods to:

- Increase the capacity of the buffer
- Get the number of available bytes as well as the total capacity of the buffer
- Consume the wrapper without losing data

`BufReader` provides methods to:

- Access the buffer through an `&`-reference without performing I/O
- Force unconditional reads into the buffer
- Get a `Read`adapter which empties the buffer and then pulls from the inner reader directly
- Shuffle bytes down to the beginning of the buffer to make room for more reading
- Get inner reader and trimmed buffer with the remaining data

`BufWriter` and `LineWriter` provides methods to:

- Flush the buffer and unwrap the inner writer unconditionally.
- Get the inner writer and trimmed buffer with the unflushed data.

[§](https://docs.rs#more-sensible-and-customizable-buffering-behavior)More Sensible and Customizable Buffering Behavior

Tune the behavior of the buffer to your specific use-case using the types in the
[ policy module](https://docs.rs/policy/index.html):

-
Refine `BufReader`’s behavior by implementing the`ReaderPolicy`trait`MinBuffered`
-
Refine `BufWriter`’s behavior by implementing the [`WriterPolicy`trait] or use an existing implementation like`FlushOn``LineWriter`

[§](https://docs.rs#making-room)Making Room

The buffered types of this crate and their `std::io` counterparts, by default, use `Box<[u8]>`
as their buffer types ([ Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html) is included as well since it is used internally
by the other types in this crate).

When one of these types inserts bytes into its buffer, via `BufRead::fill_buf()` (implicitly
called by `Read::read()`) in `BufReader`’s case or `Write::write()` in `BufWriter`’s case,
the entire buffer is provided to be read/written into and the number of bytes written is saved.
The read/written data then resides in the `[0 .. bytes_inserted]` slice of the buffer.

When bytes are consumed from the buffer, via `BufRead::consume()` or `Write::flush()`,
the number of bytes consumed is added to the start of the slice such that the remaining
data resides in the `[bytes_consumed .. bytes_inserted]` slice of the buffer.

The `std::io` buffered types, and their counterparts in this crate with their default policies,
don’t have to deal with partially filled buffers as `BufReader` only reads when empty and
`BufWriter` only flushes when full.

However, because the replacements in this crate are capable of reading on-demand and flushing less than a full buffer, they can run out of room in their buffers to read/write data into even though there is technically free space, because this free space is at the head of the buffer where reading into it would cause the data in the buffer to become non-contiguous.

This isn’t technically a problem as the buffer could operate like `VecDeque` in `std` and return
both slices at once, but this would not fit all use-cases: the `Read::fill_buf()` interface only
allows one slice to be returned at a time so the older data would need to be completely consumed
before the newer data can be returned; `BufWriter` could support it as the `Write` interface
doesn’t make an opinion on how the buffer works, but because the data would be non-contiguous
it would require two flushes to get it all, which could degrade performance.

The obvious solution, then, is to move the existing data down to the beginning of the buffer
when there is no more room at the end so that more reads/writes into the buffer can be issued.
This works, and may suit some use-cases where the amount of data left is small and thus copying
it would be inexpensive, but it is non-optimal. However, this option is provided
as the `.make_room()` methods, and is utilized by [ policy::MinBuffered](https://docs.rs/policy/struct.MinBuffered.html)
and

[.](https://docs.rs/policy/struct.FlushExact.html)

`policy::FlushExact`[§](https://docs.rs#ringbuffers--slice-deque-feature)Ringbuffers / `slice-deque` Feature

Instead of moving data, however, it is also possible to use virtual-memory tricks to
allocate a ringbuffer that loops around on itself in memory and thus is always contiguous,
as described in [the Wikipedia article on Ringbuffers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_buffer#Optimization).

This is the exact trick used by [the  slice-deque crate](https://crates.io/crates/slice-deque),
which is now provided as an optional feature

`slice-deque` exposed via the
`new_ringbuf()` and `with_capacity_ringbuf()` constructors added to the buffered types here.
When a buffered type is constructed using one of these functions, `.make_room()` is turned into
a no-op as consuming bytes from the head of the buffer simultaneously makes room at the tail.
However, this has some caveats:-
It is only available on target platforms with virtual memory support, namely fully fledged OSes such as Windows and Unix-derivative platforms like Linux, OS X, BSD variants, etc.
-
The default capacity varies based on platform, and custom capacities are rounded up to a multiple of their minimum size, typically the page size of the platform. Windows’ minimum size is comparably quite large ( **64 KiB**) due to some legacy reasons, so this may be less optimal than the default capacity for a normal buffer (8 KiB) for some use-cases.
-
Due to the nature of the virtual-memory trick, the virtual address space the buffer allocates will be double its capacity. This means that your program will *appear*to use more memory than it would if it was using a normal buffer of the same capacity. The physical memory usage will be the same in both cases, but if address space is at a premium in your application (32-bit targets) then this may be a concern.

# memchr 2.8.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/memchr/^2.0

# memchr

This library provides heavily optimized routines for string search primitives.

Dual-licensed under MIT or the [UNLICENSE](https://unlicense.org/).

### Documentation

### Overview

- The top-level module provides routines for searching for 1, 2 or 3 bytes in the forward or reverse direction. When searching for more than one byte, positions are considered a match if the byte at that position matches any of the bytes.
- The `memmem`sub-module provides forward and reverse substring search routines.

In all such cases, routines operate on `&[u8]` without regard to encoding. This
is exactly what you want when searching either UTF-8 or arbitrary bytes.

### Compiling without the standard library

memchr links to the standard library by default, but you can disable the
`std` feature if you want to use it in a `#![no_std]` crate:

```
[]
 = {  = "2",  = false }
```
On `x86_64` platforms, when the `std` feature is disabled, the SSE2 accelerated
implementations will be used. When `std` is enabled, AVX2 accelerated
implementations will be used if the CPU is determined to support it at runtime.

SIMD accelerated routines are also available on the `wasm32` and `aarch64`
targets. The `std` feature is not required to use them.

When a SIMD version is not available, then this crate falls back to
[SWAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SWAR) techniques.

### Minimum Rust version policy

This crate's minimum supported `rustc` version is `1.61.0`.

The current policy is that the minimum Rust version required to use this crate
can be increased in minor version updates. For example, if `crate 1.0` requires
Rust 1.20.0, then `crate 1.0.z` for all values of `z` will also require Rust
1.20.0 or newer. However, `crate 1.y` for `y > 0` may require a newer minimum
version of Rust.

In general, this crate will be conservative with respect to the minimum supported version of Rust.

### Testing strategy

Given the complexity of the code in this crate, along with the pervasive use
of `unsafe`, this crate has an extensive testing strategy. It combines multiple
approaches:

- Hand-written tests.
- Exhaustive-style testing meant to exercise all possible branching and offset calculations.
- Property based testing through `quickcheck`
- Fuzz testing through `cargo fuzz`
- A huge suite of benchmarks that are also run as tests. Benchmarks always confirm that the expected result occurs.

Improvements to the testing infrastructure are very welcome.

### Algorithms used

At time of writing, this crate's implementation of substring search actually has a few different algorithms to choose from depending on the situation.

- For very small haystacks,
[Rabin-Karp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabin%E2%80%93Karp_algorithm)is used to reduce latency. Rabin-Karp has very small overhead and can often complete before other searchers have even been constructed.
- For small needles, a variant of the
["Generic SIMD"](http://0x80.pl/articles/simd-strfind.html#algorithm-1-generic-simd)algorithm is used. Instead of using the first and last bytes, a heuristic is used to select bytes based on a background distribution of byte frequencies.
- In all other cases,
[Two-Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-way_string-matching_algorithm)is used. If possible, a prefilter based on the "Generic SIMD" algorithm linked above is used to find candidates quickly. A dynamic heuristic is used to detect if the prefilter is ineffective, and if so, disables it.

### Why is the standard library's substring search so much slower?

We'll start by establishing what the difference in performance actually
is. There are two relevant benchmark classes to consider: `prebuilt` and
`oneshot`. The `prebuilt` benchmarks are designed to measure---to the extent
possible---search time only. That is, the benchmark first starts by building a
searcher and then only tracking the time for *using* the searcher:

```
$ rebar rank benchmarks/record/x86_64/2023-08-26.csv --intersection -e memchr/memmem/prebuilt -e std/memmem/prebuilt
Engine                       Version                   Geometric mean of speed ratios  Benchmark count
------                       -------                   ------------------------------  ---------------
rust/memchr/memmem/prebuilt  2.5.0                     1.03                            53
rust/std/memmem/prebuilt     1.73.0-nightly 180dffba1  6.50                            53
```
Conversely, the `oneshot` benchmark class measures the time it takes to both
build the searcher *and* use it:

```
$ rebar rank benchmarks/record/x86_64/2023-08-26.csv --intersection -e memchr/memmem/oneshot -e std/memmem/oneshot
Engine                      Version                   Geometric mean of speed ratios  Benchmark count
------                      -------                   ------------------------------  ---------------
rust/memchr/memmem/oneshot  2.5.0                     1.04                            53
rust/std/memmem/oneshot     1.73.0-nightly 180dffba1  5.26                            53
```
**NOTE:** Replace `rebar rank` with `rebar cmp` in the above commands to
explore the specific benchmarks and their differences.

So in both cases, this crate is quite a bit faster over a broad sampling of benchmarks regardless of whether you measure only search time or search time plus construction time. The difference is a little smaller when you include construction time in your measurements.

These two different types of benchmark classes make for a nice segue into
one reason why the standard library's substring search can be slower: API
design. In the standard library, the only APIs available to you require
one to re-construct the searcher for every search. While you can benefit
from building a searcher once and iterating over all matches in a single
string, you cannot reuse that searcher to search other strings. This might
come up when, for example, searching a file one line at a time. You'll need
to re-build the searcher for every line searched, and this can [really
matter](https://blog.burntsushi.net/bstr/#motivation-based-on-performance).

**NOTE:** The `prebuilt` benchmark for the standard library can't actually
avoid measuring searcher construction at some level, because there is no API
for it. Instead, the benchmark consists of building the searcher once and then
finding all matches in a single string via an iterator. This tends to
approximate a benchmark where searcher construction isn't measured, but it
isn't perfect. While this means the comparison is not strictly
apples-to-apples, it does reflect what is maximally possible with the standard
library, and thus reflects the best that one could do in a real world scenario.

While there is more to the story than just API design here, it's important to
point out that even if the standard library's substring search were a precise
clone of this crate internally, it would still be at a disadvantage in some
workloads because of its API. (The same also applies to C's standard library
`memmem` function. There is no way to amortize construction of the searcher.
You need to pay for it on every call.)

The other reason for the difference in performance is that
the standard library has trouble using SIMD. In particular, substring search
is implemented in the `core` library, where platform specific code generally
can't exist. That's an issue because in order to utilize SIMD beyond SSE2
while maintaining portable binaries, one needs to use [dynamic CPU feature
detection](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/arch/index.html#dynamic-cpu-feature-detection), and that in turn requires platform specific code.
While there is [an RFC for enabling target feature detection in
 core](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3469), it doesn't yet exist.

The bottom line here is that `core`'s substring search implementation is
limited to making use of SSE2, but not AVX.

Still though, this crate does accelerate substring search even when only SSE2
is available. The standard library could therefore adopt the techniques in this
crate just for SSE2. The reason why that hasn't happened yet isn't totally
clear to me. It likely needs a champion to push it through. The standard
library tends to be more conservative in these things. With that said, the
standard library does use some [SSE2 acceleration on  x86-64](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/bf9229a2e366b4c311f059014a4aa08af16de5d8/library/core/src/str/pattern.rs#L1719-L1857) added
in

[this PR](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/103779). However, at the time of writing, it is only used for short needles and doesn't use the frequency based heuristics found in this crate.

**NOTE:** Another thing worth mentioning is that the standard library's
substring search routine requires that both the needle and haystack have type
`&str`. Unless you can assume that your data is valid UTF-8, building a `&str`
will come with the overhead of UTF-8 validation. This may in turn result in
overall slower searching depending on your workload. In contrast, the `memchr`
crate permits both the needle and the haystack to have type `&[u8]`, where
`&[u8]` can be created from a `&str` with zero cost. Therefore, the substring
search in this crate is strictly more flexible than what the standard library
provides.

# slice-deque 0.2.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/slice-deque/^0.2

# Slice Deque

A double-ended queue that

`Deref`s into a slice, also known as a ring buffer or circular buffer.

## Advantages

The main advantages of [ SliceDeque](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceDeque.html) are:

-
nicer API: since it `Deref`s to a slice, all operations that work on slices (like`sort`) "just work" for`SliceDeque`.
-
efficient: as efficient as a slice (iteration, sorting, etc.), more efficient in general than `VecDeque`.

## Platform Support

Windows, Linux, MacOS and every other unix-like OS is supported (although maybe untested). The following targets are known to work and pass all tests:

### Linux

- aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
- arm-unknown-linux-gnueabi
- arm-unknown-linux-musleabi
- armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf
- armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf
- i586-unknown-linux-gnu
- i686-unknown-linux-gnu
- i686-unknown-linux-musl
- mips-unknown-linux-gnu
- mips64-unknown-linux-gnuabi64
- mips64el-unknown-linux-gnuabi64
- mipsel-unknown-linux-gnu
- powerpc-unknown-linux-gnu
- powerpc64-unknown-linux-gnu
- powerpc64le-unknown-linux-gnu
- x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
- x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
- aarch64-linux-android
- arm-linux-androideabi
- armv7-linux-androideabi
- x86_64-linux-android

### MacOS X

- i686-apple-darwin
- x86_64-apple-darwin

### Windows

- x86_64-pc-windows-msvc

## Drawbacks

The main drawbacks of [ SliceDeque](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceDeque.html) are:

-
"constrained" platform support: the operating system must support virtual memory. In general, if you can use `std`, you can use`SliceDeque`
-
global allocator bypass: `SliceDeque``SliceDeque``VecDeque`
-
smallest capacity constrained by the allocation granularity of the OS: some operating systems allow `SliceDeque`

When shouldn't you use it? In my opinion, if

- you need to target `#[no_std]`, or
- you can't use it (because your platform doesn't support it)

you must use something else. If.

- your ring-buffer's are very small,

then by using [ SliceDeque](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceDeque.html) you might be trading memory for performance. Also,

- your application has many short-lived ring-buffers,

the cost of the system calls required to set up and grow the [ SliceDeque](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceDeque.html)s
might not be amortized by your application (update: there is a pull-request open
that caches allocations in thread-local heaps when the feature

`use_std` is
enabled significantly improving the performance of short-lived ring-buffers, but
it has not been merged yet). Whether any of these trade-offs are worth it or not
is application dependent, so don't take my word for it: measure.## How it works

The double-ended queue in the standard library ([ VecDeque](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.VecDeque.html)) is implemented
using a growable ring buffer (

`0` represents uninitialized memory, and `T`
represents one element in the queue):```
// [ 0 | 0 | 0 | T | T | T | 0 ]
//               ^:head  ^:tail
```
When the queue grows beyond the end of the allocated buffer, its tail wraps around:

```
// [ T | T | 0 | T | T | T | T ]
//       ^:tail  ^:head
```
As a consequence, [ VecDeque](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.VecDeque.html) cannot

`Deref` into a slice, since its elements
do not, in general, occupy a contiguous memory region. This complicates the
implementation and its interface (for example, there is no `as_slice` method -
the [method returns a pair of slices) and has negative performance consequences (e.g. need to account for wrap around while iterating over the elements).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.VecDeque.html#method.as_slices)

`as_slices`This crates provides [ SliceDeque](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceDeque.html), a double-ended queue implemented with
a growable

*virtual*ring-buffer.

A virtual ring-buffer implementation is very similar to the one used in
`VecDeque`. The main difference is that a virtual ring-buffer maps two
adjacent regions of virtual memory to the same region of physical memory:

```
// Virtual memory:
//
//  __________region_0_________ __________region_1_________
// [ 0 | 0 | 0 | T | T | T | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | T | T | T | 0 ]
//               ^:head  ^:tail
//
// Physical memory:
//
// [ 0 | 0 | 0 | T | T | T | 0 ]
//               ^:head  ^:tail
```
That is, both the virtual memory regions `0` and `1` above (top) map to the same
physical memory (bottom). Just like `VecDeque`, when the queue grows beyond the
end of the allocated physical memory region, the queue wraps around, and new
elements continue to be appended at the beginning of the queue. However, because
`SliceDeque` maps the physical memory to two adjacent memory regions, in virtual
memory space the queue maintais the ilusion of a contiguous memory layout:

```
// Virtual memory:
//
//  __________region_0_________ __________region_1_________
// [ T | T | 0 | T | T | T | T | T | T | 0 | T | T | T | T ]
//               ^:head              ^:tail
//
// Physical memory:
//
// [ T | T | 0 | T | T | T | T ]
//       ^:tail  ^:head
```
Since processes in many Operating Systems only deal with virtual memory
addresses, leaving the mapping to physical memory to the CPU Memory Management
Unit (MMU), [ SliceDeque](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceDeque.html) is able to

`Deref`s into a slice in those systems.This simplifies [ SliceDeque](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceDeque.html)'s API and implementation, giving it a performance
advantage over

[in some situations.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.VecDeque.html)

`VecDeque`In general, you can think of [ SliceDeque](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceDeque.html) as a

`Vec` with `O(1)` `pop_front`
and amortized `O(1)` `push_front` methods.## License

This project is licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0, (LICENSE-APACHE or [http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license (LICENSE-MIT or [http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

## Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in SliceDeque by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.
